passages.q: Why do serious accidents usually need several things to go wrong at once?
p: The psychologist James Reason proposed a simple picture of how accidents happen in complex systems such as hospitals, airlines and power plants. Imagine each layer of defence, such as training, equipment checks, alarms and procedures, as a slice of Swiss cheese. Each slice has holes, because no defence is perfect.

Most of the time, a hole in one slice is blocked by the next. An accident happens only when the holes in several slices briefly line up, letting a hazard pass straight through. A tired nurse, a confusing label and a broken alarm might each be harmless alone, but together they can lead to the wrong drug being given.

The model changes how organisations respond to mistakes. Blaming the last person in the chain does little, because the holes in the other slices remain. Investigations instead look for weaknesses in every layer and ask how to shrink or move the holes. The aim is a system in which one person’s inevitable error is caught before it causes harm.
g: Reason pictured each layer of safety as a slice of Swiss cheese, because every defence has weaknesses.
Accidents happen only when the weaknesses of several layers line up, so small harmless failures can combine.
So blaming the last person is not enough, and organisations should fix weaknesses in every layer.
k: Each layer of defence is like a slice of Swiss cheese with holes.
Accidents happen when holes in several layers line up.
Fix weaknesses in every layer rather than just blaming the last person.

mc.s: What is the main idea of the Swiss cheese model?
o: Accidents usually happen when weaknesses in several defences line up
One careless person causes most accidents
Hospitals are more dangerous than airlines
mc.e: The second paragraph states this directly.

mc.s: After a medication error, which response best fits the model?
o: Review labels, alarms, staffing and procedures as well as the individual’s action
Do nothing, since errors are inevitable
Add more paperwork only for that nurse
mc.e: The model calls for looking at weaknesses in every layer.

mc.s: Why does the author call one person’s error “inevitable”?
o: People always make some mistakes, so systems must catch them
mc.e: The final sentence assumes errors will happen and asks systems to catch them.

A defence is a protection, here a layer of safety.

passages.q: Is procrastination a problem of laziness or of something else?
p: Procrastination is often treated as poor time management or laziness. Many psychologists now describe it differently: as a way of managing unpleasant feelings. When a task makes us anxious, bored or doubtful, putting it off brings immediate relief, even though it makes things worse later.

This explains why people procrastinate on tasks that matter to them, not just on trivial ones. A report that might be judged harshly, or an email that requires an awkward conversation, triggers discomfort. Scrolling a phone removes that discomfort instantly. The brain rewards the escape, which makes the habit stronger.

If procrastination is about feelings, then the fix is not just a better calendar. Useful approaches include making the first step tiny, so starting feels less threatening; being curious rather than harsh about the discomfort; and noticing that the feeling usually fades once work begins. Research also suggests that forgiving yourself for past procrastination can make you less likely to repeat it.
g: Procrastination is often less about laziness and more about escaping unpleasant feelings.
That is why people delay important tasks, because those trigger discomfort and avoidance is instantly rewarded.
So fixes should target feelings: tiny first steps, curiosity, and self-forgiveness.
k: Procrastination is often a way to escape unpleasant feelings about a task.
Important tasks trigger more discomfort, and avoidance is rewarded instantly.
Make first steps tiny, be curious about discomfort, and forgive past delays.

mc.s: What is the passage’s view of procrastination?
o: It is mainly a way of managing unpleasant feelings
It is solved by better calendars alone
mc.e: The first paragraph reframes it as emotion management.

mc.s: You keep avoiding writing a difficult proposal. What does the passage suggest?
o: Commit to writing just the first heading
Plan a longer session for next week
mc.e: Making the first step tiny makes starting less threatening.

mc.s: Why does scrolling a phone strengthen procrastination?
o: It gives instant relief, which rewards the escape
mc.e: The second paragraph says the brain rewards the escape.

v.d: Trivial means of little importance.

o: seeming likely to cause harm or discomfort
v.d: Threatening here means feeling risky or intimidating.

passages.q: Why are electric cars more energy-efficient than petrol cars?
p: A petrol engine is a heat engine. It burns fuel to create hot gases that push pistons. Most of the energy in the fuel, often around seventy per cent or more, is lost as heat through the exhaust and the radiator rather than moving the car.

An electric motor works differently. It uses magnetic forces to turn the wheels directly, and typically converts around ninety per cent of the electrical energy it receives into motion. Electric cars can also recover some energy when braking, using the motor as a generator to recharge the battery, whereas a petrol car turns braking energy into wasted heat in its brakes.

That does not settle every question about the environmental impact. It matters how the electricity is generated: power from coal produces far more emissions than power from wind or solar. Making batteries also requires energy and mined materials. But studies that count these factors generally find that electric cars produce lower lifetime emissions in most countries, and the gap grows as electricity becomes cleaner.
g: Petrol engines waste most of their fuel’s energy as heat because they are heat engines.
Electric motors convert most energy into motion and recover braking energy, so they are far more efficient.
Environmental impact also depends on electricity sources and batteries, but studies generally favour electric cars.
k: Petrol engines lose most fuel energy as heat.
Electric motors are about 90% efficient and can recover braking energy.
Electricity source and battery making matter, but lifetime emissions usually favour electric cars.

o: Why electric cars use energy more efficiently, and what else affects their impact
How to charge an electric car
mc.e: It compares efficiency, then adds wider factors.

mc.e: The third paragraph says emissions depend on how electricity is generated.

o: Adds complications without reversing the conclusion
mc.e: It notes other factors, then says studies still generally favour electric cars.

v.d: To convert energy is to change it from one form to another.

v.d: Lifetime emissions are those over a product’s entire life, from making it to scrapping it.

passages.q: Are people less likely to help when others are around?
p: In 1964 the murder of Kitty Genovese in New York was reported as having been witnessed by 38 people who did nothing. Later investigations found that account was badly exaggerated: fewer people saw the attack, and some did call for help. But the story inspired important research.

The psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané ran experiments in which participants heard someone apparently having a seizure. People who believed they were the only witness usually went to help. Those who believed several others could also hear were slower and less likely to act. The researchers called this the bystander effect, explained partly by a diffusion of responsibility: each person assumes someone else will act.

More recent research suggests the picture is more nuanced. In clearly dangerous emergencies, groups may help as often as individuals, and analysis of real public incidents captured on camera has found that someone intervenes in most cases. The practical lesson still holds: in an emergency, point at a specific person and give them a specific task.
g: The Kitty Genovese story was exaggerated, but it inspired research on why people fail to help.
Experiments showed people help less when they think others are present, because responsibility spreads out.
Recent work finds the effect is weaker in real emergencies, but assigning a specific person a task still helps.
k: The Genovese “38 witnesses” account was exaggerated but sparked research.
Darley and Latané found people help less when others are present: diffusion of responsibility.
Real-world evidence is more nuanced; still, assign a specific person a specific task.

o: The bystander effect is real in some settings but more nuanced than once thought
The Genovese story was entirely accurate
Groups always help more than individuals
mc.e: It presents the classic finding and then the nuance from recent research.

o: Each person assumes someone else will act
Responsibility is given to the police
mc.e: The second paragraph defines it.

passages.q: Who gains and who loses when prices rise?
p: Inflation means that a pound buys less than it used to. If prices rise by ten per cent in a year, the same shopping basket costs ten per cent more. But inflation does not hurt everyone equally. Some people lose a great deal, while others can even gain.

Savers holding cash lose out if the interest they earn is below the inflation rate, because the real value of their savings shrinks. People on fixed incomes, such as some pensions, find their money stretches less far. Borrowers, by contrast, can benefit: if wages and prices rise, a fixed debt becomes smaller relative to income, so it is easier to repay.

Governments with large debts can benefit in the same way, which is one reason independent central banks were created to resist the temptation to let inflation run high. Unexpected inflation creates the biggest shifts, because people did not plan for it. Steady, predictable low inflation lets contracts, wages and interest rates adjust in advance, which is why central banks aim for it.
g: Inflation reduces what money buys, but its effects are uneven across people.
Savers and fixed-income earners lose, while borrowers can gain because debts shrink relative to income.
Indebted governments also gain, so central banks are independent and aim for predictable low inflation.
k: Inflation reduces money’s buying power, unevenly.
Savers and fixed incomes lose; borrowers can gain as debts shrink in real terms.
Unexpected inflation causes the biggest shifts; central banks aim for steady low inflation.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How inflation affects different groups differently
mc.e: It describes winners and losers and why predictability matters.

mc.s: Why might a government with large debts be tempted by inflation?
o: Inflation shrinks the real value of its debt
mc.e: The third paragraph says indebted governments can benefit like borrowers.

mc.s: Why does unexpected inflation cause bigger shifts?
o: People did not plan for it in contracts and rates
mc.e: The third paragraph explains this.

o: incomes that do not change with prices
v.d: A fixed income stays the same amount even when prices rise.

o: a strong wish to do something that may be unwise
v.d: A temptation is the pull to do something you perhaps should not.

passages.t: How an open encyclopedia stays reliable
passages.q: How can an encyclopedia that anyone can edit be reasonably accurate?
p: When Wikipedia launched in 2001, many experts expected it to fill with errors and vandalism. An encyclopedia that anyone could edit, without credentials, seemed to invite mistakes. Yet it grew into one of the most visited websites in the world and is widely used as a starting point for research.

Its accuracy rests on several mechanisms. Every change is recorded and can be reversed in seconds. Volunteers watch pages they care about and automated tools flag obvious vandalism. Articles are expected to cite published, reliable sources, and claims without sources can be challenged or removed. Disputes are discussed on separate talk pages, with written policies guiding decisions.

The system is not flawless. Coverage is uneven, reflecting who has time to volunteer, and less-watched pages can carry errors for long periods. Its own guidance says it should not be cited as a final source. The lesson is that openness can produce quality, but only when combined with transparency, sourcing rules and active community oversight.
g: Experts expected an open encyclopedia to fail, yet Wikipedia became hugely used.
It stays accurate because edits are reversible, watched, checked by tools and must cite sources.
It is not flawless, so openness works only with transparency, sourcing rules and oversight.
k: Wikipedia was expected to fail but became widely used.
Reversible edits, watchers, bots, citation rules and talk pages maintain quality.
Coverage is uneven and it is not a final source; openness needs oversight.

mc.s: What is the passage’s main point?
o: Openness can produce quality when combined with strong checks
mc.e: The final sentence summarises this.

mc.s: Why might a page about an obscure topic be less accurate?
mc.e: The third paragraph says less-watched pages can carry errors longer.

mc.s: Where are disputes about articles discussed?
mc.e: The second paragraph mentions talk pages.

a mistake caused by not noticing

passages.q: If mountains are closer to the Sun, why are their peaks colder?
p: A mountain peak is a few kilometres nearer the Sun than the valley below, but the Sun is about 150 million kilometres away, so that difference is meaningless. The real explanation lies in how the atmosphere is heated.

Sunlight passes through the air largely without warming it. It warms the ground, and the ground then warms the air above it. Air near the surface is also squeezed by the weight of all the air above, so it is denser. As air rises, the pressure falls, the air expands, and expanding air cools. On average, temperature drops by about six and a half degrees Celsius for every kilometre of height.

This is why snow can sit on peaks near the equator, such as Mount Kilimanjaro, while the plains below are hot. It also explains why climbers at high altitude face both cold and thin air. The same physics drives cloud formation: rising air cools until its water vapour condenses into droplets.
g: Mountain tops are not colder because of distance from the Sun, since the extra closeness is negligible.
Air is heated from the ground, and rising air expands and cools, so temperature falls about 6.5°C per kilometre.
So high peaks hold snow even near the equator, and the same cooling forms clouds.
k: Being slightly closer to the Sun makes no meaningful difference.
The ground heats the air; rising air expands and cools, about 6.5°C per km on average.
Hence snow on equatorial peaks, thin cold air for climbers, and cloud formation.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
mc.e: It dismisses the distance idea and explains heating and expansion.

mc.s: Why does the author mention the Sun’s distance?
o: To dismiss a tempting but wrong explanation
mc.e: The first paragraph sets aside the distance idea.

mc.s: Roughly how much does temperature drop per kilometre of height?
mc.e: The second paragraph gives this figure.

v.d: Water vapour condenses when it turns into liquid droplets.

passages.q: Why was treating zero as a number such an important step?
p: Many ancient civilisations could count and calculate, but few treated zero as a number in its own right. The Babylonians used a placeholder symbol to show an empty position in a number, so that 205 was not confused with 25, but they did not calculate with it.

In India, mathematicians went further. In 628 CE the mathematician Brahmagupta set out rules for zero as a number: adding zero to a number leaves it unchanged, and a number minus itself is zero. Combined with the Indian place-value system, in which a digit’s value depends on its position, this created the decimal numerals the world uses today.

These numerals spread to the Arab world, where scholars such as al-Khwarizmi wrote about them, and from there to Europe, where they eventually replaced Roman numerals. Try multiplying CCXLVII by XIX to see why. Place value with zero made arithmetic fast enough for trade, accounting and later algebra and computing. It is one of the most useful ideas ever recorded.
g: Some ancient cultures used zero only as a placeholder, not as a number.
Indian mathematicians, including Brahmagupta in 628 CE, treated zero as a number, so with place value it created modern numerals.
The numerals spread via the Arab world to Europe, which made arithmetic fast enough for trade and later computing.
k: Babylonians used zero only as a placeholder.
Brahmagupta (628 CE) gave rules for zero as a number; with place value this gave decimal numerals.
The numerals spread via Arab scholars to Europe and made arithmetic fast and practical.

o: How zero as a number, with place value, created modern numerals
mc.e: It traces zero from placeholder to number to global numerals.

mc.s: Why does the author suggest multiplying Roman numerals?
o: To show how much harder arithmetic is without place value
mc.e: The difficulty of the exercise shows the advantage of place value.

mc.e: The first paragraph gives the example of 205 and 25.

v.d: A placeholder marks an empty position so other digits keep their value.

v.d: Eventually means after some time.

passages.q: Do the least skilled people really overrate themselves the most?
p: In 1999 the psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger published a study in which people who scored lowest on tests of logic, grammar and humour greatly overestimated how well they had done. Those in the bottom quarter, on average, rated themselves above the middle. The researchers suggested that the skills needed to do a task well are often the same skills needed to judge how well you did it.

The finding became famous as the Dunning-Kruger effect, and it is often summarised as “stupid people think they are smart”. That summary goes too far. In the original data, almost everyone rated themselves as above average, and top performers slightly underestimated themselves. Some researchers have also argued that part of the pattern is a statistical artefact that appears when imperfect self-estimates are compared with scores.

What remains useful is a modest point: self-assessment is unreliable, especially in areas where we lack knowledge. The practical response is to seek feedback and objective measures rather than trusting how competent we feel. Feeling sure and being right are different things, for experts and beginners alike.
g: Dunning and Kruger found the lowest scorers greatly overrated themselves, perhaps because judging a skill needs that skill.
The popular summary goes too far, because almost everyone overrated themselves and part of the pattern may be statistical.
So the useful point is modest: self-assessment is unreliable, so seek feedback and objective measures.
k: Low scorers in the 1999 study greatly overestimated their performance.
The popular “stupid people think they are smart” version overstates it; part may be a statistical artefact.
Self-assessment is unreliable; seek feedback and objective measures.

mc.s: What is the author’s main point?
o: The effect is often overstated, but self-assessment really is unreliable
mc.e: The passage corrects the popular version and keeps a modest lesson.

mc.e: The second paragraph says top performers slightly underestimated.

v.d: A statistical artefact is a pattern created by how data is analysed, not by a real effect. (Also spelled artifact.)

v.d: Competent means capable and skilled enough.

passages.q: Why did customers reject a cola that tasted better in tests?
p: In 1985 Coca-Cola replaced its century-old recipe with a sweeter formula, soon nicknamed New Coke. The decision followed extensive research: in blind taste tests involving around two hundred thousand people, many preferred the new taste to both the old one and to rival Pepsi.

The public reaction was fierce. The company received tens of thousands of angry calls and letters. Some people stockpiled the old drink. Within about three months, Coca-Cola brought back the original as “Coca-Cola Classic”. The new formula faded away.

The research had answered the wrong question. Taste tests measured which drink people liked in a single sip, not how they felt about a brand tied to memories, identity and tradition. Customers felt something they owned had been taken from them. The episode is still taught as a lesson in the difference between what people prefer in a test and what they value in their lives.
g: Coca-Cola replaced its formula in 1985 after taste tests showed many preferred the new taste.
The public reacted angrily, so the company brought back the original within about three months.
The tests measured a sip, not attachment to the brand, which shows test preference differs from real value.
k: New Coke launched in 1985 after big blind taste tests favoured it.
Public anger forced the original’s return within about three months.
Taste tests missed emotional attachment to the brand.

mc.e: The final sentence states the lesson.

mc.e: The third paragraph says tests measured a single sip, not brand feelings.

passages.q: How does a lithium-ion battery store and release energy?
p: The battery in your phone works by moving charged lithium atoms, called ions, back and forth between two electrodes: a positive one, usually made of a metal oxide, and a negative one, usually graphite. Between them sits a liquid or gel called the electrolyte, which lets ions pass but not electrons.

When you charge the battery, electricity pushes lithium ions from the positive side to the negative side, where they nestle between layers of graphite. When you use the phone, the ions travel back. Each ion that moves releases an electron, which cannot cross the electrolyte, so it flows through the phone’s circuits instead. That flow of electrons is the current that powers the device.

Batteries wear out partly because each cycle causes small side reactions and physical stress that slowly reduce how many ions can move. Heat speeds this up, which is why leaving a phone in a hot car is bad for it. Many phones now slow charging near full, because spending long periods at one hundred per cent also adds stress.
g: A lithium-ion battery moves lithium ions between two electrodes through an electrolyte that blocks electrons.
Charging pushes ions to the graphite side, and using the battery lets them return, so released electrons flow through the device as current.
Batteries wear out through side reactions and stress, so heat and long periods at full charge shorten their life.
k: Lithium ions move between electrodes through an electrolyte that blocks electrons.
Charging moves ions to the graphite; discharging moves them back, sending electrons through the circuit.
Side reactions, heat and long periods at full charge wear batteries out.

o: How lithium-ion batteries work and why they wear out

passages.t: How chess masters see the board
passages.q: What makes experts so much better at remembering in their field?
p: In the 1970s the psychologists William Chase and Herbert Simon showed chess positions to players for a few seconds and asked them to rebuild the positions from memory. Masters were far better than novices, placing most pieces correctly while beginners managed only a few.

But when the pieces were arranged randomly, in positions that could not occur in a real game, the masters’ advantage largely vanished. Their memory was not generally better. Instead, years of play had given them a huge store of familiar patterns, so they saw a position as a handful of meaningful groups, or chunks, rather than as many separate pieces.

Chunking helps explain expertise in many fields. An experienced doctor sees a pattern of symptoms, an experienced investor recognises a familiar type of deal. This is also why expertise is so specific: the chunks come from the domain itself. Building expertise means accumulating patterns through extensive practice and feedback, not training a general-purpose memory.
g: Chess masters remembered real positions far better than novices after a brief look.
Their advantage vanished with random positions, because their skill was recognising familiar chunks, not better memory.
Chunking explains expertise in many fields, so it is specific and built through practice and feedback in the domain.
k: Masters recalled real chess positions far better than novices.
With random positions the advantage vanished: they recognise chunks, not remember better.
Expertise is domain-specific pattern knowledge built through practice and feedback.

mc.e: The random-position result shows it is pattern knowledge, not general memory.

passages.q: How does a message travel across the internet?
p: When you send a photo over the internet, it does not travel as one piece. Your device breaks it into many small chunks of data called packets. Each packet carries part of the photo plus a header, which includes the address it is going to and its place in the sequence.

Packets are passed between routers, computers whose job is to forward them towards their destination. Each router looks at the address and sends the packet on by whatever route seems best at that moment. Packets from the same photo may take different paths across the network and arrive out of order. At the other end, the receiving device reassembles them in the right sequence and asks again for any that went missing.

This design, called packet switching, was developed in the 1960s partly to make networks robust. If one link fails, packets simply flow around it. It also lets many users share the same lines efficiently, because no one occupies a connection while silent. The approach remains the foundation of the internet today.
g: Data is split into small packets, each with an address and position in sequence.
Routers forward each packet along the best available route, so packets may arrive out of order and are reassembled.
Packet switching makes networks robust and efficient, so it remains the internet’s foundation.
k: Data is split into packets with headers containing address and order.
Routers forward packets by changing routes; the receiver reassembles them and requests missing ones.
Packet switching is robust and shares lines efficiently; it underpins the internet.

o: How the internet moves data in packets

passages.q: Do workers improve simply because someone is watching?
p: Between the 1920s and 1930s, researchers at the Hawthorne Works, a factory near Chicago, studied how lighting and other conditions affected productivity. According to the famous story, output rose whether the lights were turned up or down, apparently because the workers knew they were being studied. This became known as the Hawthorne effect.

Later researchers re-examined the original data and found the story much shakier than its fame suggests. Some apparent effects could be explained by other changes, such as different pay systems or the replacement of workers, and the lighting experiments were never formally published.

Still, the broader idea is reasonable and important for anyone running an experiment. People may behave differently when they know they are observed, and simply receiving attention or a new routine can change behaviour for a while. Good studies guard against this with comparison groups that receive the same attention but not the actual change being tested.
g: The Hawthorne studies supposedly found output rose with any lighting change because workers knew they were observed.
Later analysis found the story shaky, because other changes may explain the results.
Still, being observed can change behaviour, so good studies use comparison groups with equal attention.
k: The Hawthorne story: productivity rose with any change, supposedly due to observation.
Re-analysis found the evidence shaky; other factors may explain it.
Observation can still affect behaviour; comparison groups with equal attention guard against it.

passages.q: How did India become one of the world’s great tea producers?
p: In the early nineteenth century, Britain drank enormous quantities of tea, almost all of it bought from China. The trade was costly and depended on China’s willingness to sell. The British East India Company looked for ways to grow tea in territories it controlled.

In the 1820s and 1830s, the Singpho people and others in Assam were found to use a local tea plant, and British officials eventually confirmed it as a variety of the tea plant. The Company also smuggled seeds, plants and expertise from China. In 1839 the first Assam tea was auctioned in London, and plantations spread rapidly across Assam and later Darjeeling and the Nilgiris.

The industry was built on harsh conditions. Workers were recruited, often deceptively, from other regions and faced low pay and restrictive contracts. Today India is among the largest tea producers in the world, and tea is part of daily life across the country, but historians remind readers that its plantation origins involved significant hardship.
g: Britain depended on costly Chinese tea, so the East India Company sought to grow its own.
A local Assam tea plant and smuggled Chinese expertise led to plantations from 1839 onward.
The industry grew huge but was built on harsh, often deceptive labour practices.
k: Britain relied on Chinese tea and wanted its own supply.
Local Assam tea and smuggled Chinese plants led to the first auction in 1839 and rapid expansion.
India became a leading producer, but plantations relied on harsh labour.

passages.q: Why do people on the same flight pay very different prices?
p: Two passengers sitting side by side on a plane may have paid wildly different fares. This is not an accident. Airlines deliberately charge different prices to different customers for essentially the same seat, a practice economists call price discrimination.

The aim is to charge each customer close to what they are willing to pay. Business travellers who book late and need flexibility will often pay a lot; holidaymakers who book months ahead and can choose dates are more price-sensitive. Airlines separate these groups using conditions such as booking time, refundability and whether the stay includes a weekend. Software adjusts prices constantly as seats sell.

Price discrimination can seem unfair, but it can also widen access. High fares from some customers can help fund cheaper seats for others, filling planes that would otherwise fly with empty seats. Cinemas with student discounts and software with different plans for individuals and companies use the same logic. The key is separating groups who value the product differently.
g: Passengers pay different fares for the same seat because airlines deliberately use price discrimination.
Airlines charge each group near what it will pay, using conditions like booking time to separate them.
It can seem unfair but can widen access, and many businesses use the same logic of separating groups.
k: Airlines charge different prices for the same seat: price discrimination.
They target willingness to pay using booking time, refundability and stay conditions.
It can fund cheaper seats and fill planes; cinemas and software use it too.

o: Why and how businesses charge different customers different prices
mc.e: It explains price discrimination, its methods and its effects.

mc.e: Conditions like refundability separate high-willingness customers.

o: A shop charging everyone the same
mc.e: The final paragraph gives student discounts as an example.

passages.q: How can a pill with no active ingredient make people feel better?
p: In clinical trials, some patients are given a placebo: a dummy treatment, such as a sugar pill, that looks identical to the real drug. Patients on placebos often report real improvements, particularly in symptoms such as pain, nausea and fatigue.

Part of this placebo effect comes from expectation. Believing a treatment will help can change how the brain processes pain signals, and brain scans have shown changes linked to placebo pain relief. The ritual of care, such as being examined and given treatment by a confident clinician, also seems to matter. Even the colour and price of pills can influence how well people say they work.

Not all apparent placebo improvement is caused by the placebo. Many conditions improve naturally, and symptoms that are unusually bad when people seek help tend to ease afterwards. Placebos do not shrink tumours or cure infections. This is why trials compare a drug with a placebo: a treatment only counts as effective if it does better than the placebo.
g: Patients on dummy treatments often report real improvements in symptoms like pain.
Expectation and the ritual of care drive part of this, because belief changes how the brain processes symptoms.
Some improvement is natural recovery and placebos do not cure disease, so drugs must beat placebos in trials.
k: Placebos often produce reported improvements, especially in pain and nausea.
Expectation and the ritual of care influence how the brain processes symptoms.
Some change is natural recovery; placebos don’t cure disease; trials compare drugs against them.

o: What the placebo effect is, what drives it, and its limits
mc.e: It covers the effect, its causes and its limits.

mc.e: The final paragraph explains that a drug must do better than the placebo.

v.d: A dummy treatment imitates the real one but has no active ingredient.

v.d: A ritual is a set of actions carried out in a set, meaningful way.

passages.q: Why is a magnitude 7 earthquake so much bigger than a magnitude 6?
p: News reports describe earthquakes by magnitude, such as 5.8 or 7.1. These numbers can mislead, because the scale is not like a ruler. Each step of one whole number represents a very large jump.

Modern seismologists mainly use the moment magnitude scale. On it, an increase of one unit means the ground shaking measured on instruments is about ten times larger, and the energy released is roughly thirty-two times greater. So a magnitude 7 earthquake releases around a thousand times more energy than a magnitude 5. This kind of scale, in which each step multiplies rather than adds, is called logarithmic.

Magnitude still does not tell the whole story of damage. A moderate earthquake directly beneath a crowded city with weak buildings can kill far more people than a larger one in a remote area or a country with strict building codes. Depth matters too: shallow earthquakes generally cause stronger shaking at the surface.
g: Earthquake magnitudes mislead because each whole number is a big jump, not an even step.
On the moment magnitude scale each unit means about 32 times more energy, so the scale is logarithmic.
Damage also depends on location, buildings and depth, not magnitude alone.
k: The magnitude scale is not linear; each step is a big jump.
Each unit is about 10× the measured shaking and about 32× the energy: a logarithmic scale.
Damage also depends on location, building quality and depth.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How the magnitude scale works and what else affects damage
mc.e: It explains the scale, then adds factors beyond magnitude.

mc.s: About how much more energy does a magnitude 8 release than a magnitude 7?
mc.e: Each unit is roughly 32 times more energy.

mc.e: The third paragraph explains this.

increasing by adding the same amount

passages.q: Does a child’s ability to wait for a treat predict their future?
p: In the 1960s and 1970s, the psychologist Walter Mischel offered young children at a Stanford nursery a choice: one marshmallow now, or two if they could wait alone for several minutes. Follow-up studies years later found that children who waited longer tended to have better outcomes in adolescence, including school results.

The finding became famous as evidence that self-control in early childhood predicts later success. But the original samples were small and drawn from children of university staff. In 2018 a larger study of a more diverse group of children found a much weaker link, and much of that link disappeared once family background and early abilities were taken into account.

Other research suggests that waiting also depends on trust. Children who had just experienced an adult breaking a promise waited far less, which is a rational choice if rewards seem unreliable. The modern view is not that self-control is unimportant, but that a single test of waiting says less about a child’s future than once believed, and much about their circumstances.
g: Mischel found that children who waited for two marshmallows tended to have better outcomes later.
But the samples were small and narrow, and a larger 2018 study found a much weaker link.
Waiting also depends on trust and circumstances, so one test predicts less than once thought.
k: Children who waited longer tended to do better later in Mischel’s studies.
A larger, diverse 2018 study found a much weaker link, largely explained by background.
Waiting depends on trust and circumstances; the test predicts less than believed.

mc.e: It describes the original finding and later evidence that weakened it.

passages.q: Why have so many businesses moved to subscriptions?
p: Software that was once sold in a box for a one-off price is now often rented by the month. Razors, meal kits, cars and even socks are offered on subscription. The shift is driven by what subscriptions do to a company’s revenue.

One-off sales must be won again every time. Subscription revenue recurs automatically until a customer cancels, which makes it more predictable and easier to plan around. Investors tend to value predictable revenue highly. Subscriptions also give companies an ongoing relationship with customers, with steady data about how products are used and chances to sell upgrades.

The economics depend on two numbers: how much it costs to acquire a customer, and how long they stay. If customers cancel quickly, the business may never earn back what it spent attracting them. That is why subscription companies obsess over “churn”, the share of customers leaving each month, and why some make cancelling deliberately difficult, a practice regulators increasingly challenge.
g: Many products have shifted from one-off sales to subscriptions because of what it does to revenue.
Subscriptions bring predictable recurring revenue and an ongoing customer relationship, which investors value.
Success depends on acquisition cost and customer lifetime, so firms fight churn, sometimes unfairly.
k: Many products have moved to subscriptions.
Recurring revenue is predictable, valued by investors, and gives ongoing data and upsell chances.
The model depends on acquisition cost versus lifetime; churn is critical.

mc.e: It covers the appeal and the key economics.

passages.q: Why do we add a day to the calendar every few years?
p: The Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun. A calendar of exactly 365 days would slowly drift: after a century the seasons would arrive almost a month later than the dates suggested.

The Julian calendar, introduced under Julius Caesar in 46 BCE, solved most of this by adding a day every four years. But a year is actually slightly shorter than 365.25 days, by about eleven minutes. Over centuries those minutes added up, and by the sixteenth century the calendar had drifted by about ten days.

In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII introduced a reformed calendar. It removed ten days at once and changed the rule: years divisible by 100 are not leap years unless they are also divisible by 400. So 1900 was not a leap year, but 2000 was. Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar only in 1752, by which time it had to skip eleven days.
g: A 365-day calendar would drift from the seasons because the orbit takes about 365.25 days.
The Julian calendar added a day every four years, but a year is slightly shorter, so it drifted ten days.
The Gregorian reform removed days and skipped some century leap years, and Britain adopted it in 1752.
k: The orbit takes about 365.25 days, so a 365-day calendar drifts.
The Julian calendar’s four-year leap day overshot by about 11 minutes a year.
The Gregorian calendar (1582) skips century leap years not divisible by 400.

o: Why leap years exist and how the rules were refined
mc.e: It covers the problem, the Julian fix and the Gregorian refinement.

Yes, because it is divisible by 4

passages.q: Why does the Arctic tern fly so far each year?
p: The Arctic tern is a small seabird, weighing around a hundred grams. Each year it flies from its breeding grounds in the Arctic to the Antarctic and back again. Tracking devices have shown that some birds travel more than 70,000 kilometres a year, the longest known regular migration of any animal.

The journey is not a straight line. Terns follow winding routes that take advantage of prevailing winds, and they stop in rich feeding areas in the ocean to refuel. Over a lifetime that can last thirty years, a tern may fly a distance equivalent to several trips to the Moon and back.

Why go so far? By breeding in the Arctic summer and spending the rest of the year in the Antarctic summer, terns experience more daylight than any other animal. Long days mean long hours for catching fish. The extreme journey is a strategy for following abundant food and light around the planet.
g: The tiny Arctic tern migrates from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back, over 70,000 km a year.
It follows winding, wind-assisted routes with feeding stops, so over a lifetime it covers enormous distances.
It goes so far because two polar summers give maximum daylight for fishing.
k: Arctic terns migrate pole to pole, some over 70,000 km a year.
Routes wind with prevailing winds and include feeding stops.
They chase two summers of long daylight for feeding.

o: How and why the Arctic tern makes the longest migration
mc.e: It describes the journey, its route and its purpose.

mc.s: Why don’t terns fly in a straight line?

mc.e: The second paragraph explains this.

mc.s: What advantage does the migration bring?
mc.e: The third paragraph links it to daylight and feeding.

v.d: Prevailing winds are the ones that usually blow in a region.

passages.q: Why do larger teams often become slower?
p: Adding people to a team adds capacity, but it also adds conversations. In a team of three, there are three possible pairs of people who need to coordinate. In a team of six, there are fifteen. In a team of twelve, there are sixty-six. The number of connections grows much faster than the number of people.

Each connection carries a cost: meetings, messages, misunderstandings and waiting for agreement. Beyond a certain size, much of a team’s time goes on coordinating rather than doing. The software engineer Fred Brooks observed in 1975 that adding people to a late software project tends to make it later, because newcomers need training and add communication overhead.

This is why many organisations deliberately keep teams small and give them clear ownership of a goal. Amazon’s founder Jeff Bezos popularised the idea of a “two-pizza team”, small enough to be fed by two pizzas. The point is not the pizza but the principle: fewer, clearer connections let a team decide and act quickly.
g: Adding people adds connections much faster than people: 3 for three, 15 for six, 66 for twelve.
Each connection costs time, so big teams spend more time coordinating, and adding people can delay projects.
So organisations keep teams small with clear ownership, like two-pizza teams, to act quickly.
k: Connections grow much faster than headcount (3, 15, 66).
Coordination costs time; Brooks: adding people to a late project makes it later.
Small teams with clear ownership, e.g. two-pizza teams, act faster.

o: Coordination costs grow quickly with team size, so small teams can move faster
mc.e: The passage builds from the maths of connections to the principle of small teams.

mc.e: The formula is n × (n − 1) ÷ 2, so 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10.

v.d: Overhead is the extra cost or effort that does not directly produce output.

passages.q: How does cricket set a fair target when rain shortens a match?
p: In one-day cricket, the team batting second chases a target set by the first team’s score over fifty overs. If rain cuts the second innings short, simply scaling the target by overs is unfair. A team might score most of its runs late in an innings, when batters take more risks, and wickets matter as much as overs.

In 1997 the statisticians Frank Duckworth and Tony Lewis introduced a method based on the idea of “resources”. A team’s resources at any point are the combination of overs remaining and wickets in hand. Using historical data, the method estimates what share of its total resources a team has used or lost, and adjusts the target accordingly.

The method, later refined by Steven Stern and now called Duckworth-Lewis-Stern, is not perfect and is often misunderstood by fans. But it is much fairer than the simple alternatives it replaced, one of which famously left South Africa needing an impossible 21 runs from one ball in the 1992 World Cup semi-final.
g: Scaling a target by overs is unfair because scoring is uneven and wickets matter too.
Duckworth and Lewis based targets on resources, combining overs and wickets, using historical data.
The refined DLS method is imperfect but fairer than the old rules that produced absurd targets.
k: Scaling targets by overs alone is unfair.
Duckworth-Lewis uses resources: overs remaining plus wickets in hand, from historical data.
Now DLS; imperfect but far fairer than earlier methods (e.g. 1992 semi-final).

How to bowl in the rain

passages.q: How does a solar panel turn light into electricity?
p: A solar panel is made of many cells, usually based on silicon. Each cell has two layers of silicon treated with small amounts of other elements, so that one layer has extra electrons and the other has spaces where electrons are missing. Where the layers meet, an electric field forms.

When sunlight hits the cell, its energy knocks electrons loose from silicon atoms. The electric field at the junction pushes these freed electrons in one direction. If wires connect the two sides of the cell, the electrons flow through them as current. This is called the photovoltaic effect.

Typical commercial panels convert around a fifth of the sunlight that hits them into electricity; the rest becomes heat or reflects away. Output changes with clouds and time of day, and stops at night, which is why solar power is increasingly paired with batteries. The cost of solar panels has fallen dramatically over recent decades, making them one of the cheapest sources of new electricity in many places.
g: Solar cells use two treated silicon layers that create an electric field where they meet.
Sunlight frees electrons and the field pushes them, so connected wires carry current: the photovoltaic effect.
Panels convert about a fifth of sunlight, vary with conditions and need batteries, but costs have fallen sharply.
k: Solar cells have two treated silicon layers with an electric field at the junction.
Light frees electrons; the field drives them through a circuit: the photovoltaic effect.
About 20% efficient, variable, often paired with batteries; costs have fallen dramatically.

passages.q: How can a simple checklist reduce deaths in surgery?
p: Surgery involves teams of skilled professionals working under pressure. Even experts occasionally forget a routine step: confirming the patient’s identity, checking for allergies, or making sure antibiotics are given at the right time. Each lapse is rare, but across millions of operations they add up.

In 2008 a team working with the World Health Organization introduced a one-page Surgical Safety Checklist in eight hospitals around the world, from London to Delhi. Teams paused at three points, before anaesthesia, before the first incision and before the patient left the theatre, to confirm key items aloud. A study published in 2009 reported that deaths and major complications fell substantially after the checklist was introduced.

Part of the benefit came from the items themselves. Part came from the conversation: introducing every team member by name and role made it easier for a junior nurse to speak up if something seemed wrong. Results in later studies have varied with how seriously hospitals used it, but the checklist is now standard in many countries. Its lesson reaches beyond medicine: simple tools can catch the errors that expertise alone misses.
g: Even expert surgical teams occasionally skip routine steps, and these rare lapses add up.
The WHO checklist made teams pause and confirm key items, and a 2009 study reported fewer deaths and complications.
Its benefit came from both the items and better team communication, so simple tools can catch errors experts miss.
k: Experts occasionally skip routine steps; across many operations this matters.
The WHO checklist adds three pauses; a 2009 study reported large falls in deaths and complications.
